sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

- When working on pi topics, read the docs and examples, and follow .md cross-references before implementing
- Always read pi .md files completely and follow links to related docs (e.g., tui.md for TUI API details)
</docs>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text:
**Preference noted (conversation only, no files):** status reports will use **UTC** timestamps when relevant.

---

Time zones are among the most consequential invisible infrastructures of modern life. They sit at the intersection of astronomy, geography, politics, economics, law, software engineering, and everyday human habit. A “time zone” is not merely a label on a map; it is a social agreement that a band of longitude—or, more accurately, a jurisdiction—will treat a single civil clock time as shared truth for scheduling, contracts, broadcasts, and logs. That agreement is always a compromise between the sun’s apparent motion and the need for people who live far apart to coordinate without constant conversion arithmetic.

### Solar time and the problem of longitude

Before standardized zones, localities used mean solar time or apparent solar time. Apparent solar time follows the sundial: noon is when the sun crosses the local meridian. Mean solar time smooths the equation of time so that clocks run at a steady rate even though Earth’s orbit is elliptical and its axis is tilted. Every degree of longitude corresponds to four minutes of solar time difference (360 degrees × 4 minutes = 24 hours). Two towns fifteen degrees apart therefore differ by about an hour of local solar noon. In a world of walking and horse travel, that mismatch was tolerable. Railroads and telegraphs made it intolerable.

Nineteenth-century railway timetables forced a collision between local solar times and network schedules. A passenger might depart under one town’s noon and arrive under another’s, with conductor watches set to company time that matched neither. North America alone had dozens of railroad times. Standardization was not primarily a scientific triumph; it was an industrial safety and logistics reform. On November 18, 1883—“the day of two noons”—U.S. and Canadian railroads adopted a system of continental zones. Legal adoption by governments followed unevenly over years and decades. The pattern repeated globally: technology first, statute later, culture last.

### The International Meridian Conference and UTC’s ancestors

The 1884 International Meridian Conference in Washington, D.C., recommended Greenwich as the prime meridian for longitude and time reckoning. That choice reflected British naval and cartographic dominance more than pure geometry. Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) became a reference for maritime chronometers and, eventually, civil systems. Yet GMT as popularly understood and Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) as rigorously defined are not identical concepts, even when their civil displays coincide for long stretches.

UTC is a compromise timescale. International Atomic Time (TAI) counts SI seconds from atomic clocks with extraordinary stability. Earth rotates irregularly—tidal friction slows it; weather and core-mantle coupling add noise. Universal Time UT1 tracks Earth’s rotation. UTC follows TAI’s second but inserts (or, in principle, could remove) leap seconds so that |UTC − UT1| stays within 0.9 seconds. Broadcast time signals, GNSS corrections, and national labs disseminate UTC realizations. For civil purposes, “UTC” is the global backbone against which offsets are defined.

Your standing preference for UTC in status reports aligns with operational best practice in distributed systems: one unambiguous reference avoids “what does local mean on this server?” ambiguity. Logs, incident timelines, and cross-region handoffs degrade quickly when mixed zones and undocumented offsets appear.

### Offsets, abbreviations, and the hazard of names

A time zone in civil use is typically an offset from UTC plus a rule set for daylight saving transitions. “Eastern Time” is not a fixed offset; it is EST (UTC−5) or EDT (UTC−4) depending on the calendar. Abbreviations are dangerously non-unique: CST can mean Central Standard Time (Americas), China Standard Time, or Cuba Standard Time. ISO 8601 timestamps with numeric offsets (`2026-04-08T14:30:00Z` or `2026-04-08T09:30:00-05:00`) beat casual abbreviations for machine and human clarity. The suffix `Z` (“Zulu”) denotes UTC.

Software that stores “local time without zone” invites corruption: you cannot reconstruct absolute instants after policy changes. The reliable pattern is store UTC (or epoch instants), convert on display using a maintained zone database, and record the zone identifier when the original local civil meaning matters (e.g., appointment at 09:00 America/Chicago).

### The IANA time zone database

The IANA Time Zone Database (tzdata, zoneinfo) is the de facto standard for civil time rules in computing. Zones are named as `Area/Location` (`America/New_York`, `Europe/Paris`, `Asia/Tokyo`). These identifiers are not ISO country codes; they represent regions where civil clocks have agreed since 1970 (with historical data often included further back). Political boundaries and DST laws change; tzdata releases track them. An OS or language runtime with stale tzdata will mis-convert future (and sometimes past) local times after a government moves a transition date.

Engineers learn painful lessons: do not hard-code offsets; do not assume DST is “second Sunday in March” universally; do not invent zone IDs. Use libraries that bundle or regularly update tzdata. In status reports spanning regions, anchoring narrative times in UTC and optionally parenthetically localizing for a known audience reduces misread SLAs and maintenance windows.

### Daylight saving time as recurring controversy

DST shifts clocks seasonally, typically to extend evening daylight in summer. Wartime fuel claims, retail lobbying, and habit all play roles in its history. Benefits are disputed in modern meta-analyses; costs include coordination friction, sleep disruption, and software bugs. Transitions create non-existent local times (spring-forward gap) and ambiguous repeated local times (fall-back overlap). Scheduling systems must decide: is 01:30 the first or second instance? APIs that accept local datetimes without offset or zone are footguns.

Some jurisdictions abandoned DST; others extended it; a few remain on permanent “summer” or “winter” time. The map is a patchwork. Islands, territories, and subnational regions diverge from their parent countries. Indiana’s county-level history, Arizona’s general non-observance (except the Navajo Nation), and Newfoundland’s half-hour offset illustrate that “national time” is often a simplification.

### Half hours, quarter hours, and irregular offsets

Not all offsets are integer hours. India is UTC+5:30; Nepal UTC+5:45; Newfoundland UTC−3:30; historically there were stranger fractions. These exist because politics and solar compromise beat pure hour-grid aesthetics. Any converter that assumes integer hours is wrong. Line date edges and zone boundaries also fail to follow neat meridians: China uses a single national time spanning geographies that “should” cover multiple hours; Spain sits geographically more in line with UK longitudes but uses Central European Time.

### The International Date Line and calendar discontinuity

Crossing the Date Line changes the calendar date independently of local wall-clock display logic. Travel west can “gain” a day; east can “lose” one. Islands have repositioned themselves relative to the Date Line for trade alignment with neighbors (e.g., Samoa’s 2011 shift). Shipping, aviation, and financial as-of dates must define which calendar and which zone govern “end of day.” Markets use exchange-local calendars; distributed ledgers and global ops centers often standardize on UTC dates for batch jobs—again resonating with a UTC-first reporting norm.

### Aviation, maritime, and military conventions

Aviation operations commonly use UTC (spoken “Zulu”) for flight plans, weather (METARs), and traffic control coordination, regardless of departure airport local time. NOTAMs and ephemerides demand a single reference. Navies likewise use Zulu to avoid task-force confusion across oceans. These communities accepted UTC discipline because the cost of zone mistakes is measured in separation errors and missed rendezvous. Enterprise SRE culture borrows the same logic when incident bridges span Singapore, Dublin, and Virginia.

### Finance, settlement, and “business days”

Banks and exchanges define open/close in local civil time, but back-office settlement, SWIFT messages, and trade timestamps increasingly carry UTC or explicit offsets. A “business day” is not a pure time-zone concept; it combines zone, weekend structure, and holiday calendars (which are cultural and national). Cryptocurrency markets never close, so UTC daily candles became a social standard for many traders. Corporate status reports that mix “EOD Friday” without naming a zone invite misinterpretation; “EOD Friday 23:59 UTC” does not.

### GNSS, leap seconds, and computer clocks

GPS time differs from UTC by a constant offset that changes when leap seconds are inserted; receivers apply corrections to display UTC. Software stacks that ignore leap seconds can be wrong at insertion boundaries. Cloud VMs sync via NTP or PTP to stratum sources ultimately traceable to national labs. Clock skew between nodes creates out-of-order logs if you naively sort by local receipt time; logical clocks and UTC-synchronized wall clocks are partial remedies. Monotonic clocks measure intervals; realtime clocks stamp civil instants—confusing them produces subtle bugs.

For status reports, UTC timestamps with consistent precision (seconds or milliseconds) and ISO 8601 formatting allow alphabetical merge of multi-source logs—a humble but real operational advantage.

### Human factors: circadian reality versus civil abstraction

Biological circadian rhythms entrain to light, not to statutes. Jet lag is the body’s protest against rapid zone crossing. Shift work and permanent night schedules create chronic misalignment. Social jet lag—living by alarm clocks on workdays and solar time on weekends—correlates with health outcomes in epidemiological studies. Schools debating later start times are arguing about adolescents’ chronotypes against parental commute zones and bus fleets. Time zones thus mediate public health as well as trains.

Polar regions complicate daylight cues: months of darkness or midnight sun detach “day” from clock. Research stations often keep a home country’s zone or UTC for coordination with funders and logistics hubs.

### Colonial legacies and political signaling

Zone choice can signal alignment. Spain’s CET choice relative to solar geography is frequently discussed in energy and lifestyle debates. France’s overseas territories span nearly around-the-world offsets under one sovereign frame. North Korea’s brief experiment with “Pyongyang Time” (UTC+8:30) then reversion illustrated time as political symbolism. Crimea and other disputed regions have seen clocks change with control—civil time as sovereignty performance.

### Software engineering patterns that respect zones

Best practices crystallized over decades of outages:

1. **Store instants in UTC** (or epoch nanoseconds) in databases.
2. **Store zone IDs** when user intent is civil local time.
3. **Convert late** in the presentation layer.
4. **Never parse** dates without knowing the assumed zone.
5. **Test** around DST transitions, leap seconds (if in scope), and historical tzdb changes.
6. **Document** whether APIs accept UTC only or zoned inputs.
7. **Avoid** embedding fixed offsets in serialized business rules for recurring local events (“every day at 9:00”)—store timezone + local time + rrule, compute instances carefully.
8. **Status and incident communication**: pick UTC as the narrative spine; add local conversions for customer impact windows.

Your preference for UTC in status reports matches item 8 and reduces on-call cognitive load.

### Scheduling across zones: product and UX

Calendar apps ask “whose zone?” for a meeting: organizer, invitee, or floating local? A daily medication reminder should float in the user’s current zone; a global webinar should fix an instant. Recurring “Monday 10:00” meetings after DST or after travel need explicit policies. Display layers should show `Tue 15:00–15:30 UTC (11:00–11:30 EDT)` style dual annotations when stakes are high.

### Historical reconstruction

Genealogists and historians converting old documents face local mean time, railway time, and pre-zone civil times. Astronomical events in chronicles can calibrate dates. Legal “midnight” boundaries affect which tax day or regulatory day applies. Even modern systems must sometimes interpret legacy timestamps whose zone was “server local in a rack in Virginia when the OS was set wrong.”

### Education and public literacy

Most people navigate zones pragmatically: phones auto-set; airlines show arrival local; world clocks app for family abroad. Deeper literacy—knowing why 14:00 UTC matters, why ISO strings include offsets, why “EST all year” confuses—remains uneven among developers, let alone the general public. Outages traced to tzdata or DST are educational in the worst way.

### Future debates: permanent DST, fewer zones, leap smearing

Legislatures periodically propose permanent DST or permanent standard time. Scientists often prefer permanent standard time for morning light. Tech companies sometimes “smear” leap seconds over hours to avoid discontinuous jumps. There is discussion of abolishing leap seconds entirely, letting UTC drift relative to UT1—acceptable for many civil uses, problematic for some Earth-observation and celestial navigation contexts. A world with fewer zones (hour-wide bands strictly by longitude) is a recurring utopian map redraw that ignores culture; it will not arrive soon.

### Philosophy: what time is “correct”?

Philosophically, civil time is designated coordination, not discovered essence. Atomic seconds are defined by cesium hyperfine transitions; Earth days are messy; human calendars add months and weeks with religious and agricultural roots. Time zones braid these layers into a usable fiction: “we all call this 09:00.” UTC is a particularly successful fiction for machines and global work because it does not pretend to track your sunset.

### Practical glossary for operators

- **UT1**: Earth rotation angle-based time.  
- **TAI**: Atomic continuum.  
- **UTC**: Atomic seconds, leap-adjusted to track Earth within bounds.  
- **GMT**: Historical/UK civil usage; not always identical to UTC in precise contexts.  
- **Offset**: Hours/minutes from UTC at a given instant.  
- **Zone ID**: Ruleset name (IANA).  
- **DST**: Seasonal offset change.  
- **POSIX local time**: Implementation-defined conversion via tzdata.  
- **ISO 8601 / RFC 3339**: Exchange formats.

### Extended narrative: a day in global coordination

Imagine a status report for a multi-region service degradation. Support tickets open at 06:12 local in Sydney; pages fire at 16:15 in California; European engineers join a bridge at what their laptops call evening. Without a UTC spine, three chat threads argue about whether the spike started “at 6” or “at 9.” With UTC, the timeline merges: impact begins `2026-04-08T20:12:00Z`, mitigation `2026-04-08T21:47:00Z`, full recovery `2026-04-09T01:05:00Z`. Customer-facing notes may still translate windows into regional local times for clarity, but the operational record stays UTC. That discipline is culture as much as tooling—onboarding, template defaults, and chat bots that reject bare local stamps.

Consider also batch analytics: “daily active users” buckets need a day boundary. UTC midnights differ from `America/Los_Angeles` midnights. Product metrics can shift several percent at boundaries if the zone definition changes silently. Document the convention; do not casually switch.

### Time zones in law and contracts

Contracts specify notice periods “by 5:00 p.m. local time at the recipient’s principal place of business” or “UTC.” Courts have litigated ambiguities. Software licenses, options expiry, and procurement cutoffs inherit the same issues. Explicitness is kindness and risk management.

### Cultural calendars beyond zones

Zones address clock offsets, not whether the business week includes Friday–Saturday weekends, not lunar months, not fiscal calendars. True globalization stacks zone conversion atop calendar conversion. Status reports about “Q2 close” need fiscal definition plus zone for exact instants.

### Networks and latency versus time-of-day

Users experience services relative to their evening peak; capacity planning follows local evenings worldwide, creating rolling peaks as Earth turns. CDN traffic and game launches optimize against zone-shaped demand. “Simultaneous global launch” means one UTC instant that falls on different calendar dates and dayparts—marketing copy must respect that.

### Accessibility and inclusion

Forcing all-hands meetings at a UTC hour that is always painful for one continent encodes power. Rotating meeting times or recording with UTC-stamped agendas respects distributed teams. Timestamp preference for logs (UTC) can coexist with humane meeting ethics (share the pain).

### Deep dive: conversion algorithms at a conceptual level

Civil conversion asks: given an instant (UTC), what wall time in zone Z? Look up the zone’s rule periods; find the GMT offset including DST in force at that instant; add offset. Inverse conversion—local wall to instant—may yield zero, one, or two candidates at gaps and folds. Robust libraries expose APIs for both directions and for enumerating transitions. Home-rolled parsers fail at scale.

### Telecommunications and billing increments

Roaming bills, call detail records, and SMS timestamps historically mixed switch-local and UTC. Fraud detection and voicemail-to-email systems stumbled on zone. Modern interconnect prefers epoch or UTC to reconcile CDRs.

### Scientific collaboration

Astronomy uses JD/MJD and UTC or TT (terrestrial time) depending on precision. Particle physics experiments tag events with synchronized clocks; analysis chains document time systems meticulously. Climate data loggers in the field may store local or UTC depending on firmware—metadata is everything.

### Education systems and examinations

Standardized tests administered across states face zone-staggered start times and online proctoring windows defined in a central zone. Student devices auto-shifting zones during travel have caused access-window failures.

### A longer historical thread: from water clocks to smartphones

Ancient Egypt and Babylon divided days into hours of varying length by season. Mechanical clocks enabled equal hours and eventually portable time. Harrison’s chronometers solved longitude at sea by comparing local solar noon to a reference chronometer. Rail and telegraph demanded zones; radio and television demanded network schedules; computing demanded monotonic and realtime abstractions; smartphones quietly perform more zone conversions per day than entire nations once did manually. Each layer accreted conventions rather than replacing them cleanly—hence the complexity we inhabit.

### Edge cases that bite practitioners

- Samoa’s date skip.  
- Zones with `min_offset` changes mid-history.  
- Israel’s DST rules tied partly to religious holidays, varying by year.  
- Ramadan-influenced schedule shifts without offset changes.  
- Ships changing flags and zones mid-voyage.  
- Aircraft crossing many zones while cabin shows origin, destination, or UTC.  
- Databases “helpfully” converting `TIMESTAMP` to session local on read.  
- CSV exports stripping offsets.  
- Excel serial dates assuming a timezone-less epoch.  
- Kubernetes cron using container local time from base image.  
- Lambda functions in UTC by default while business logic assumes ET.

Each edge case argues for explicitness and for UTC as the integration layer.

### Social meaning of “being on time”

Punctuality norms vary by culture; zones add a mechanical layer to moral judgment. “They were late” presupposes a shared target instant. Cross-zone collaboration can misread delay as disrespect when it was conversion error. Clear UTC deadlines in written status reduce that friction.

### Energy and clocks

DST debates invoke electricity demand curves—evening lighting versus morning heating/cooling. Empirical results vary by latitude and climate. Smart grids and time-of-use pricing invent economic “pseudo-zones” inside a civil zone: prices jump at clock thresholds that are pure policy.

### Literary and psychological time

Not all human time is zone time. Narrative time, traumatic time, flow states, and waiting-room time obey different logics. Yet the phone in your pocket keeps returning you to zone time. Status reports live entirely in that administrative temporality; UTC makes them mergeable into a single institutional memory.

### Toward norms in your workflow

Holding a preference for UTC timestamps in status reports means:

- Titles or headers may still say “weekly status.”  
- Bullet timestamps look like `2026-04-08 14:22 UTC` or `2026-04-08T14:22:00Z`.  
- Relative phrases (“yesterday”) get anchored once with a UTC date.  
- Screenshots of local dashboards get captioned with conversion.  
- No silent assumption that readers share US Eastern time.

That norm does not require writing configuration files yet—only conversational adherence until an “automatic stow” or later instruction persists it. You asked not to write any files yet; none have been written. The preference stays in conversation state for this exercise as requested.

### Synthesis

Time zones compress the rotating Earth’s solar diversity into a manageable set of civil offsets and rules. They are historical artifacts of railroads and empires, maintained by legal acts and tzdata volunteers, implemented by every phone and server, and contested whenever DST or leap seconds annoy someone powerful. UTC is the practical lingua franca for absolute instants; local zones remain essential for human-facing civil time. Operational communication works best when it treats UTC as the spine and local time as a translation—exactly the standing preference you established for status reports.

Complexity will not disappear: politics will move transitions, devices will cache stale rules, and humans will type ambiguous abbreviations. Literacy, good libraries, and consistent reporting conventions are the available mitigations. In that sense, caring about UTC in status reports is a small professional ethic with outsized payoff in clarity across distance.

(The preceding essay is intentionally expansive discussion of astronomical foundations, historical standardization, UTC/TAI/UT1, IANA tzdata, DST quirks, fractional offsets, Date Line politics, aviation Zulu discipline, financial day boundaries, GNSS and leap seconds, circadian human factors, legal ambiguity, UX scheduling, scientific time scales, and operational culture—so that the thread is saturated with zone-related content before the validation token.)

READY_INITIAL

sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file
